cues.text: A Fisherman Called from His Nets
The son of Zebedee and Salome, a family of evident means on the Sea of Galilee, James was called alongside his younger brother John .
Zebedee kept hired hands in his fishing business, while Salome herself is counted among the women who later ministered to Christ from their own resources.
The two brothers were mending their nets alongside their father.
Both brothers left everything at once.
Their fervent, sometimes impetuous temperament earned them from Christ a memorable nickname, Boanerges , "sons of thunder."
The name speaks of zeal not yet fully tamed by grace.
It was the raw material from which the Lord would shape one of his most trusted friends.
Admitted to the Inner Circle
Among the Twelve, James belonged to the smaller company of three — with Peter and his own brother John — whom Jesus drew closer than the rest at the most decisive moments of his ministry.
It was James who stood with them on the mountain of the Transfiguration , witnessing Christ's glory unveiled before Moses and Elijah.
James again accompanied Jesus deepest into the garden of Gethsemane , close enough to see the full weight of the Lord's agony before sleep overcame him.

We recognize in this privileged nearness not favoritism but formation: James was shown both the glory and the anguish of Christ's mission precisely because he would need both to sustain the calling still ahead of him.
A Request for Glory, Answered with a Cup
The Gospel does not flatter James in every scene.
Together with John, he once asked Jesus for the places of highest honor in his coming kingdom.
Jesus answered not with rebuke but with a searching question: could they drink the cup that he himself was about to drink?
Both brothers answered yes, not fully understanding what they were promising.
James's later martyrdom would prove that this rash promise, made in the confidence of youthful zeal, was one he kept in full.
The very cup of suffering he had asked to share turned out, in the end, to be exactly what was given him.
First of the Apostles to Die
The Acts of the Apostles records James's death with stark brevity: Herod Agrippa I "killed James, the brother of John, with the sword."
Agrippa was seeking to please the Jewish leadership hostile to the young Church.
Around the year 44, this made James the first of the Twelve to be martyred.
His was the only martyrdom of one of the Twelve recorded directly in the New Testament itself.
An ancient tradition preserved by Clement of Alexandria adds a detail of particular grace.
The very man who had accused James before the tribunal was so moved by the Apostle's confession of faith that he too declared himself a Christian on the spot.
The two were led away together and, according to Clement's account, suffered martyrdom.
A Journey to Spain, and a Long Afterlife
A tradition reaching back many centuries, though resting more on devotion than on documented certainty, holds that James had earlier preached the Gospel in Spain .
After his martyrdom, tradition holds, his body was carried by sea back to the Iberian peninsula, eventually coming to rest at what became Santiago de Compostela in Galicia.
Whatever the precise historical weight of this tradition, its consequences were undeniable.
By the Middle Ages, Compostela had become one of the three great pilgrimage destinations of Christendom alongside Rome and Jerusalem.

The Camino de Santiago still draws hundreds of thousands of walking pilgrims each year, many seeking, at the end of a long physical journey, something of the same total surrender James himself once promised at the water's edge.
Legacy
James remains patron of Spain, of pilgrims, and of all who travel in search of God.

His scallop shell—the emblem still worn by walkers of the Camino—remains a reminder that the Christian life itself is a kind of pilgrimage, undertaken step by faithful step toward a destination not fully seen.
The fisherman who once asked for a throne beside Christ's glory was given instead the cup of Christ's own suffering, and accepted it without flinching.
In that acceptance, he became a companion for every believer who has ever prayed for something and received instead a harder, truer gift.
He understood exactly what such a prayer can cost, and exactly what it can become.
